features: ⚠️ THIS VERSION CHANGES THE DATABASE — One new column on the supplier record, to tell «not subject to withholding» apart from «nobody has ever been asked». The migration runs automatically on upgrade, and the database backup is taken first, as always.

THE WITHHOLDING THE INVOICE DOES NOT DECLARE — A document without a withholding block does not mean none is due: the obligation belongs to the building as withholding agent, not to the supplier who writes it on the invoice. Of eleven real invoices, six do not declare it, and one of those six is from a surveyor on whom 20% is due: until now it was recorded at the full amount, silently, and the Revenue Agency received nothing. Now, the first time you record an invoice from a supplier who has never been classified, the program asks whether they are subject to withholding — once in that supplier's whole life.

THE QUESTION ARRIVES WITH AN ANSWER ALREADY IN IT — The document does carry some clues, and they are used to propose rather than to decide: if it declares the flat-rate scheme, withholding does not apply and it says so; if it declares a professional fund contribution, or if the supplier invoices as an individual rather than a company, it proposes self-employment at 20%. Every proposal explains where it comes from and stays editable: in the normal case it is a one-click confirmation.

THE PREVIEW SHOWS THE WITHHOLDING IMMEDIATELY — Answering «subject to withholding» while recording an invoice, the totals box kept saying «No withholding € 0.00» and the net stayed at the full amount: it was reading the saved supplier record instead of the answer just given. The document was then recorded correctly, but the figure shown before pressing «Record» was a different one. The preview now withholds straight away — on € 1,000.00 of taxable amount it shows € 200.00 at 20% and € 40.00 at 4%.

A «NO» IS NOW REMEMBERED TOO — «This supplier is not subject to withholding» used to be written in exactly the same way as «nobody has looked yet»: the two were indistinguishable, and such a notice could never have been dismissed. The answer now sticks, whatever it is, and the question does not come back.

AN XML FILE CAN NO LONGER BRING THE SERVER DOWN — There was no limit at all on how many lines were read from an electronic invoice: a 10 MB file produced 81,284 of them and 111 MB of memory, on installations that often have 128 in total. At most a thousand are read now — real invoices have at most six, so the margin is generous even for a utility bill with one line per meter — and the check fires before the file is even opened, not after. Anyone loading such a document is told how many lines it has and why it was refused.

THE CHECK ON THE BUILDING'S TAX CODE NOW TELLS THE WHOLE STORY — After an import, the notice about a missing tax code only said that without it no tax documents can be issued. True and incomplete: without that field the check that refuses an XML invoice addressed to a different building also stops working, which is the most expensive error to discover late.
